c668045c-a6ea-11f1-9fa3-9762e3473041.one_liner: A macro-trading interview arguing long-duration Treasuries are cheap despite the deficit/AI-issuance narrative, with a secondary bearish update on private credit still finding no bottom.
c668045c-a6ea-11f1-9fa3-9762e3473041.recap: Jared Dillion (Daily Dirt Nap, author of The Awesome Portfolio) argues the bond sell-off is driven by a 'mind virus' of deficit and inflation fear rather than fundamentals: inflation is falling, labor data (weak payrolls, soft ISM/JOLTS/Chicago PMI) points to a slowdown, and the deficit at ~6% of GDP is well below 2010's 12%. He notes strong auction bid-to-covers show demand is being ignored while only supply gets attention, and argues a risk-off equity shock would send yields sharply lower. He says he has moved a large share of his own money into 30s (5.3%) and 10s (4.7%) as a multi-year trade. The conversation touches Volcker-era crowding-out logic, applied now to hyperscaler debt issuance (e.g., a $40bn Google bond) pressuring yields, and disagrees mildly with a guest's (Torsten Slok-referenced) view that AI outcomes both point to lower yields. Much of the rest covers equity sentiment and single-name views: financials/semis/healthcare 'topping' on his chart review, retail concentration in Nvidia/Broadcom, the Citadel/hedge-fund semiconductor block-trade unwind, gold's pullback after Jackson Hole/Warsh remarks with support near $3,900-4,000, copper as his least-favored metal, and speculative 'baldness drug' stock ideas. On credit, he reiterates a two-year-old bearish call on private credit/private equity, saying valuations haven't bottomed because illiquid private markets reprice much more slowly than public ones, and that AI, private credit and private equity risks are interlinked.
